**Plan pl_001 — 6 items in execution order:**

| # | Item | Record type | Place / Date window | Repository |
|---|------|------------|---------------------|------------|
| pli_001 | Rowan County Probate Records, name search | Probate | Rowan Co. NC, 1839–1899 | FamilySearch collection 4000201 (name-searchable); search Voss/Foss/Voos |
| pli_002 | 1850 US Federal Census | Census | Rowan Co. NC, 1850 | FamilySearch collection 1473181 — Caroline (~11) almost certainly in father's household |
| pli_003 | NC County Marriages, 1762–1979 | Parents' marriage | Rowan Co. NC, 1820–1838 | FamilySearch collection 4000202 — confirms parents as a unit; supplies mother's maiden name |
| pli_004 | 1860 US Federal Census (FAN) | Census | Rowan Co. NC, 1860 | FamilySearch — father may still head a Voss household; surfaces siblings for collateral lines |
| pli_005 | Rowan County Probate, full-text browse | Probate (FTS fallback) | Rowan Co. NC, 1839–1899 | FamilySearch image group 004900301 — keyword "Voss" reaches ~60% the name index misses |
| pli_006 | Caroline's death certificate / burial record | Death record | Rowan Co. NC, 1913–1940 | Ancestry (NC death certs name father from 1913); Find A Grave as secondary |

---

**Rationale summary:**
North Carolina had no statewide death registration before 1913, making county probate records the primary route to a father's estate in this era. The 1850 census is the earliest name-indexed census with Caroline (~11) almost certainly in her father's household — the most direct path to his identity. The parents' marriage record corroborates the couple without proving Caroline is their child. The 1860 census catches a surviving father and surfaces siblings for collateral-line corroboration. The full-text browse (pli_005) is a fallback for the ~60% of probate entries the name index misses. Finally, if Caroline survived past 1913, her death certificate on Ancestry would typically name her father directly.

**Next step:** Run FamilySearch searches for pli_001–pli_005 (search-records), then Ancestry/Find A Grave for pli_006 (search-external-sites). Confirmation is needed before executing.

## Research Plan for q_001 — Who were the parents of Katharina Seeger (b. ~1843, Baiersbronn)?

Katharina has no parents, spouse, or sources in the tree yet. Because all relevant Protestant church registers for Baiersbronn are digitised only on **Archion** (a paid German church-archive platform), every step involves browsing images there or contacting the state archive. Nothing is indexed on FamilySearch.

**pli_001 — Familienregister (Baiersbronn, Archion, 1800–1880)**
Browse the *Familienregister* (a Württemberg household register) — it lists the head, spouse, and all children on one spread. Finding the Seeger household would name Katharina's parents in a single step. This is your most efficient starting point.

Browse sibling baptism entries in the same window. Entries for the same parents identify the family unit and godparents can serve as neighbour/associate leads.

**pli_004 — Heiratsbuch / Marriage Register (Baiersbronn, Archion, 1818–1845)**
Once you have the parents' names from steps 1–3, look up their marriage entry to get the mother's maiden name and corroborate the father. Note: this alone doesn't prove Katharina was their child — a record placing her with them is still needed.

A parent's estate file may name all children as heirs. This is a different record type at a different repository — contact the Landesarchiv directly or check their website for access details.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

**Mode: Add-new** — prior plan pl_002 was already completed; new active plan **pl_003** created for q_001 ("Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?")

---

### Existing facts the survey found

- **I1 (Patrick Flynn):** birth ~1845, Ireland (per 1850 & 1860 census); death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, PA
- **I2 (Thomas Flynn):** birth ~1818, Ireland; no independent sources
- **R1 (Thomas→Patrick, ParentChild):** supported by three quality-2 sources — 1850 & 1860 census co-residence (inferred, no relationship column) and 1908 death certificate (father named as Thomas Flynn; informant was son-in-law, secondary)
- **Birthplace conflict:** 1850/1860 censuses give Ireland; death cert gives Pennsylvania (secondary informant)
- No search has been run against Thomas Flynn's probate, church records, naturalization, deeds, or Patrick's marriage record

---

### Plan pl_003 — FAN-Cluster Approach (8 items in execution order)

| # | Item | Record Type | Place / Date | Repository | Rationale |
|---|------|-------------|--------------|------------|-----------|
| pli_006 | 1870 U.S. Census | Census | Schuylkill Co., PA, 1870 | FamilySearch | Names Thomas Flynn's household → identifies Patrick's siblings for the FAN chain |
| pli_007 | 1880 U.S. Census | Census | Schuylkill Co., PA, 1880 | FamilySearch | First census with explicit relationship-to-head column; stated "son" relationship is direct |
| pli_008 | Church records | Baptism | Schuylkill Co., PA, 1835–1875 | FamilySearch | Baptism entries name both father and mother directly; variant spellings (Flinn, Flyn) to be tried |
| pli_009 | Probate records | Probate/Will | Schuylkill Co., PA, 1861–1910 | FamilySearch (browse) | Thomas Flynn's will naming Patrick as son = strongest possible direct parentage evidence |
| pli_010 | Marriage records | Vital | Schuylkill Co., PA, 1863–1885 | FamilySearch (browse) | PA marriage licenses typically name groom's parents |
| pli_011 | Naturalization records | Immigration | Schuylkill Co., PA, 1845–1875 | FamilySearch (browse) | Thomas's declaration/petition may name wife and children; also resolves birthplace conflict |
| pli_012 | Land / deed records | Land | Schuylkill Co., PA, 1845–1900 | FamilySearch (browse) | Conveyance from Thomas to Patrick = direct evidence; FAN proximity confirmed by co-witnesses |
| pli_013 | Civil War service & pension | Military | United States, 1861–1900 | FamilySearch | Pension sworn declarations sometimes name parents directly |

---

### Why this is a FAN approach

The previous plan relied on census co-residence (inferred relationship) and a death certificate with a secondary informant — neither gives a direct, independent parentage statement. Plan pl_003 shifts strategy to:

1. **Find Thomas Flynn's other children** via his 1870/1880 households — those siblings' own records can then name Thomas as father
2. **Search church baptism registers** that explicitly name both parents
3. **Browse Thomas's probate file** for a will naming Patrick as son
4. **Check Patrick's marriage record** (PA licenses name the groom's parents)
5. **Review Thomas's naturalization papers** for a family declaration
6. **Scan land deeds** for father-to-son conveyances and FAN associations
7. **Check military pension files** where sworn declarations often name parents

Hand to **search-records** beginning with:
- **pli_006** — 1870 U.S. Census, Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill County, PA (name-searchable)

- **pli_013** — Civil War Soldiers Index (name-searchable)

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Search for children baptized to John Doyle and Bridget Halloran or Doyle in Schuylkill County Catholic parishes, which were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (later Diocese of Allentown from 1961). The birth window for Doyle children runs approximately 1858-1882.

The 1900 US Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) uniquely recorded for each married woman the number of children she had given birth to and the number still living. If Bridget survived to 1900 (she would be approximately 62), this field provides direct evidence of the total number of Doyle children she bore. Also search for adult Doyle children with their own households in Schuylkill County; children born 1858-1882 would be 18-42 years old in 1900 and likely heading their own households.

Probate records (wills, letters of administration) are held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills from 1811 (locality guide loc_001). items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn's 1908 death certificate is already cited in the project tree as S3 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates, cert no. 4521), but no parental-name assertions have been extracted from it for q_001. Pennsylvania civil death registration began in 1906 (loc_001), so the 12 March 1908 death falls within the registration period. Pennsylvania death certificates of this era include fields for the father's name and the mother's maiden name — the two unknowns q_001 seeks — as well as the informant's name. This collection is name-searchable on FamilySearch. Searching for Patrick Flynn with a death date of 1908 in Schuylkill County, with variant spelling Flyn, should surface the record directly.

Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland) last appears in the project tree in the 1860 census (S2) and could have died anywhere from 1860 through approximately 1910. The date range is bounded by Thomas's plausible lifespan, not Patrick's research window. S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is already listed in the project tree as a source but has no extracted assertions for q_001. A will naming Patrick as a son is direct paternity evidence; a will also commonly names the testator's wife, which would identify Patrick's mother. Loc_001 confirms the Register of Wills holds probate records from 1811. The FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994) is browse-only (personCount 0); image group 007936749 (Schuylkill Probate Records 1851-1930) is also browse-only (personCount 0) and must be browsed image-by-image for the Flynn surname. The county Register of Wills is the physical repository if online images are incomplete.

The 1880 U.S. census is the first federal census to state each person's relationship to the head of household explicitly. A search for Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland) in Schuylkill County in 1880 would both confirm Patrick's relationship to Thomas in the household record's own words and name Thomas's wife — Patrick's otherwise unknown mother. Patrick would be ~35 in 1880 and may have formed his own household; searching for him too is warranted. Collection 1417683 (United States Census, 1880) is name-searchable; search with variant spelling Flyn as well as Flynn.

Fallback for the 1880 census (pli_003): if Thomas Flynn cannot be found in 1880, the 1870 census is the next best option. The 1870 census does not state relationships but lists all household members by name — Thomas's wife's given name would appear alongside Patrick (age ~25 in 1870, who may still be in the household). Collection 1438024 (United States Census, 1870) is name-searchable; also available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/). Search with variant spelling Flyn.

Thomas Flynn born ~1818 would be ~82 in 1900 and could still be alive, living in his own household or with Patrick (age ~55, confirmed surviving until 1908). The 1900 census records each wife's number of children born and children living, and reports each person's parents' birthplaces — useful for confirming Irish origin for Thomas. If Thomas is deceased by 1900 and a widow is found with the Flynn surname in the household, she may be Patrick's mother. Collection 1325221 (United States Census, 1900) is name-searchable.

A dedicated search for Thomas Flynn's marriage to his wife is required for this parentage plan. Thomas and his wife likely married around 1840-1845 (before Patrick's ~1845 birth), either in Ireland before emigration or in Schuylkill County shortly after arrival. The couple's marriage record confirms them as a unit and, if this was the wife's first marriage, supplies her maiden name — the primary unknown. Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records) is name-searchable and covers Catholic registers, the likely denomination for Irish immigrants in the anthracite coal region (loc_001). If no result is found there, image group 007936751 (Schuylkill Church Records 1842-1895, browse-only (personCount 0)) should be browsed. Caution: if this was the wife's second marriage, the surname this record gives may be a prior married name rather than her birth surname; that possibility should be tested if evidence of an earlier husband is found.

Fallback for the marriage search (pli_006): if Thomas and his wife's marriage record is not found, search for Patrick Flynn's baptism or the baptisms of his siblings in Schuylkill County church records. Sibling baptisms routinely name both parents — a route to the mother's name even without the marriage entry. Patrick was born ~1845 in Ireland per the project tree (F1) and may have been baptized there before the family emigrated; a sibling born in Pennsylvania would be more likely to appear here. Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH is name-searchable; image group 007936751 (browse-only (personCount 0)) is the browse fallback.

FAN item required for this parentage question. Deed records name not only the grantor and grantee but also the adjoining landowners in the boundary recital and the witnesses — the FAN cluster (family, associates, neighbors) most likely to include kin or co-emigrants from the same Irish parish. Thomas Flynn's deeds in Schuylkill County could surface neighboring households who may be relatives, former neighbors from Ireland, or godparents — a lead toward identifying the mother or the Irish townland of origin. Image group 007936752 (Schuylkill Deed Records 1815-1900) is 22% name-searchable; use the name index first for Thomas Flynn and variant Flyn, then browse the relevant years (roughly 1845-1875 for Thomas's active period as a property holder).

Patrick Flynn born ~1845 would have been ~16-20 during the Civil War and is old enough to have enlisted near the war's end. A Civil War pension file names the soldier's wife, children, and next of kin — potentially identifying Patrick's mother or confirming Thomas as his father through the pension application. Thomas Flynn born ~1818 (~43-47 during the war) is a secondary candidate. Collection 1910717 (United States, Civil War Soldiers Index, 1861-1865) is name-searchable; if a match is found, pension files are held at NARA and are also available on Ancestry.

Swedish marriage entries of this period typically named the bride's father and often her home parish, making this the single highest-yield item for identifying Elena's parents. Search the Sweden, Marriages, 1630-1920 collection (1520596), which is name-searchable; also try name variants of Elena (Helena, Elin, Ellen, Eljena) per the Sweden Naming Customs wiki. If the national Marriages index does not carry the entry, browse image group 004523018 (Västra Karaby 1688-1804, browse-only (personCount 0)) at the December 1712 section to read the marriage entry directly from the register page. The same volume spans the 1696-1720 date range in another coverage row and would contain the full entry including any marginal notes on the bride's origin.

The christening entry for Asmund Jönsson (11 September 1718, Barsebäck) names both parents; Swedish baptism entries of this era sometimes recorded the parents' origin parish as well. The godparents named in the entry are FAN members — frequently kin of the parents — and could be Elena's relatives, providing additional leads to her family and surname. The son's given name Asmund mirrors Elena's patronymic, consistent with the Swedish naming pattern of giving the second son the name of the mother's father. Search the Sweden, Baptisms, 1611-1920 collection (1520594), which is name-searchable.

If the national Baptisms index does not carry the entry, browse image groups 004514823 and 004514824 (Barsebäck registers from 1648 onward, browse-only (personCount 0)) at the September 1718 section to read the entry directly. Note the godparents' surnames — any sharing Asmundsson or Asmundsdotter would indicate kinship with Elena's paternal family.

Full-text co-occurrence search via the search-full-text skill: pair 'Asmundsdotter' with 'Asmund' as two separate required terms, run unscoped across the entire Swedish church records corpus. Because the Malmöhus church records (1974200) are browse-only (personCount 0) and 0% name-indexed, the national name indexes cannot surface entries in those volumes; a full-text scan of AI-transcribed page text can find the marriage entry, an Asmund household in the husförhörslängd, or any Elena entry the name indexes miss. The patronymic 'Asmundsdotter' is the most distinctive anchor term; also run with abbreviated forms (Asmund d., Asmund dr., Asmund dtr.) per the Sweden Naming Customs wiki. Do not scope to any single collection.

Household tax lists (mantalsläng) recorded heads of household annually by village within each härad and are available online at https://sok.riksarkivet.se/mantalslangder covering 1642-1820. Elena's patronymic names her father's given name as Asmund; search Harjager härad (which includes Västra Karaby and Barsebäck) for a male named Asmund between approximately 1685 and 1730 to identify the specific village — and therefore the parish — where he lived. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.
